content: Corticosteroids are commonly administered to children undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) to mitigate the inflammatory response associated with the procedure. However, their use remains controversial, with decisions varying between medical centers and even among individual physicians within the same institution. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of prophylactic corticosteroid use in children, from birth to 18 years of age, undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB. The review included studies that investigated corticosteroid administration at any dose, via any route, and at any time during the perioperative period, provided the steroids were used prophylactically rather than therapeutically. Studies involving heart or lung transplantation, patients already receiving corticosteroids, or those with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis abnormalities were excluded. Additionally, studies where corticosteroids were administered for non-cardiac surgery indications were not considered. The review process involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as of June 2020. A total of 3748 studies were identified, of which 2868 unique records were screened. After reviewing the full texts of 84 studies, 13 studies were included in the analysis. Eight of these studies, involving 478 participants, were included in the meta-analysis, while the remaining five were described narratively due to the absence of events in both the intervention and placebo groups for the outcomes of interest. The findings revealed the following: 1. In-hospital mortality: Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that corticosteroids do not significantly alter the risk of in-hospital mortality in children undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB (five RCTs; 313 participants; risk ratio [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.33 to 2.07). 2. Duration of mechanical ventilation: High-certainty evidence indicated that corticosteroids reduce the duration of postoperative mechanical ventilation by an average of 11.37 hours (six RCTs; 421 participants; mean difference [MD] -11.37 hours, 95% CI -20.29 to -2.45). 3. Length of postoperative ICU stay: High-certainty evidence showed that corticosteroids likely have little to no effect on the length of ICU stay after surgery (six RCTs; 421 participants; MD -0.28 days, 95% CI -0.79 to 0.24). 4. Length of postoperative hospital stay: Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that corticosteroids probably have little to no effect on the total length of hospital stay after surgery (one RCT; 176 participants; MD -0.70 days, 95% CI -2.62 to 1.22). 5. All-cause and cardiovascular mortality at longest follow-up: Moderate-certainty evidence indicated no significant effect of corticosteroids on all-cause mortality (five RCTs; 313 participants; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.07) or cardiovascular mortality (three RCTs; 109 participants; RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.07 to 2.46) at the longest follow-up. 6. Separation from CPB: Low-certainty evidence suggested that corticosteroids likely make little to no difference in the ability of children to separate from CPB (one RCT; 40 participants; RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.92). The review was unable to provide conclusive information on adverse events due to inconsistent reporting across studies. The certainty of evidence was downgraded in several instances due to factors such as small sample sizes, reliance on single studies for specific outcomes, wide confidence intervals encompassing both potential benefit and harm, and potential publication bias. In conclusion, corticosteroids likely do not affect mortality risk in children undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB but may reduce the duration of postoperative mechanical ventilation. They appear to have little to no impact on the length of ICU or hospital stay. The lack of consistent adverse event reporting limits the ability to make definitive recommendations regarding their safety. The review underscores the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials with sufficient power to assess clinical outcomes and adverse events. Additionally, the development of a standardized core outcome set for adverse event reporting in pediatric major surgery and intensive care is essential.
